newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S&P assigns BB rating to Philippine bonds.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S&P assigns BB rating to Philippine bonds.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp said it has assigned a BB rating to a proposed issue of fixed rate 2016 bonds and floating rate 2011 bonds by the Republic of the Philippines. It said the ratings outlook was positive.
S&P said at least US$200 million of new fixed rate bonds and $200 million of new floating rate bonds may be issued in exchange for outstanding Philippine Brady bonds, also rated BB.
The new bonds will be priced on September 23 and the aggregate amount will be determined on October 1.

Interest reduction bonds due 2017 and 2018 are eligible for exchange. "Unlike the Brady bonds eligible for the exchange, which are secured as to principal by U.S. Treasury zero coupon bonds and partly secured as to interest by other high-grade securities, the new bonds will not be collateralised," S&P said.
S&P said the BB foreign currency rating of the Philippines was based on several factors, including:

- the progressive liberalisation of its economy, as privatisation and deregulation of key sectors, notably communications, power and oil, enhance the competitiveness and long term growth prospects of the economy and exports;

- modest improvements in public finances, as slightly improved tax administration, revenue measures such as the extension of value added tax (VAT), and falling interest payments have cut the underlying public sector deficit to two percent of gross domestic product in 1996;

- a manageable external debt burden, as a declining external borrowing requirement and rapidly rising exports reduce net external debt to an expected 90 percent of exports this year, net public debt to under 50 percent of exports, and the long term debt service ratio to 15 percent.
S&P said the rating remained constrained by:

- The Philippines' limited fiscal flexibility. A complex tax code and poor compliance which keeps recurrent revenues to 16 percent of GDP. "Also, public debt of 70 percent of GDP and inflexible payroll costs, which absorb nearly 40 percent of recurrent revenues, leave insufficient resources to adequately address the country's pressing infrastructure and social needs."
- low savings and investment rates of 19 percent and 22 percent of GDP respectively, which constrain economic performance relative to its neighbours

- the vulnerability of the balance of payments, as a trade deficit of 12 percent of GDP and an estimated current account deficit (adjusted for errors and ommissions) of four percent of GDP make external finances dependent on confidence-sensitive remittances from overseas workers and portfolio investment
S&P said the outlook was positive.

"Political support for the government's economic policies should allow the passage of key tax reforms proposed by the government under its Comprehensive Tax Reform Program over the medium term," the ratings agency said.

"However, opposition from powerful vested interests and weakened cooperation between the Ramos administration and Congress could still result in a dilution of the government's proposals and slippage in the implementation of other reforms crucial to fiscal consolidation," it said.

"Improvements in creditworthiness hinge on the enactment of a meaningful tax reform package, which should provide the foundation for a sustained rise in recurrent revenues and allow steady increments in public investment," it said.

"Also, Standard and Poor's expects creditworthiness to be enhanced by the more cautious monetary policy evident since last year, which should cut inflation to single digit levels and by the improved external flexibility resulting from gradually rising levels of domestic saving and foreign direct investment."
